lesson_title: How a Footpath Becomes a Canyon
hook_text: There are canyons in the Eastern Cape deep enough to swallow a bakkie. Most of them started as a cattle path.
clip_script: Topsoil is a bank account that fills at one teaspoon a year — centuries of rotting leaves, weathering rock and earthworm labour to build a few centimetres. And one thunderstorm on a bare slope can withdraw decades of it in an afternoon. Deposits by teaspoon, withdrawals by bucket. Now watch the crime happen, in five acts. Act one: too many cattle for the grass, and a patch goes bare. Act two: rain hits that bare patch like thousands of tiny hammers, splashing soil loose. Act three: the trampled ground cannot drink, so the water flows — a thin sheet quietly stealing the whole surface a millimetre at a time. Act four: the sheet gathers into little finger-channels, easy to step over, easy to ignore. Act five: the channels join, deepen with every storm, and one year the farmer cannot cross his own camp — a donga has opened, a raw canyon with cliff walls where a field used to be. And the cattle path to the dam, stamped hard as a stoep? That was the first drain. South Africa loses hundreds of millions of tonnes of topsoil a year this way, off the one-tenth of land that can actually grow food. The counterattack has names: keep ground covered, plough along the contours, rest the veld — and where a donga already gapes, wire baskets of rock called gabions go in like speed bumps, tripping each flood until it drops its stolen soil and the canyon slowly fills itself back in.
visual_style: Time-lapse animation of a green hillside degrading act by act — bare patch, splashing raindrops in macro, sheetwash shimmer, rills branching, then a yawning donga — reversed at the end as gabions appear and grass climbs back up the healing channel.
mood: Quietly ominous, forensic, ending on repair and resolve.
pacing: Slow teaspoon open, accelerating beats through the five acts, a stark pause at the open donga, steady hopeful rebuild to close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to read — and reverse — the five acts on any hillside.
